opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is to start from the environment and the user rather than from the model. People often talk about "agents" as one thing, but a coding agent, a customer-service agent, and a research agent live in very different worlds, and the design should follow from that.

One dimension is how much interaction there is with a human. Some tasks are basically "give me the goal and come back with the result," like running a long software task or a deep research report. There the agent should be autonomous, able to work for a long time, recover from its own mistakes, and the main metric is whether the final outcome is correct. Other tasks are interactive, where the human is in the loop the whole time, like a copilot in your editor or an assistant helping you shop. There, latency matters, understanding what the person actually wants matters, and asking the right clarifying question at the right moment matters more than raw autonomy. That's partly why we built benchmarks like τ-bench: a lot of real value comes from agents interacting with both tools and people, and that's much harder to evaluate than a static question-answer setup.

Another dimension is the environment itself: what actions are available, how reliable the feedback is, and how costly mistakes are. In coding you have a compiler and tests, so the agent gets dense, verifiable feedback and can try many things. In the real world, like booking a flight or sending an email, actions are irreversible, so you want more caution, confirmation, and maybe a different balance between thinking and acting.

So I don't think there's one "right" agent architecture. The underlying capabilities, reasoning with language and using tools, can be shared and general. But the product form, the interface, the reward, and the evaluation should be quite different per task. I think the next phase of this field is less about making models smarter in the abstract and more about defining good tasks and good environments, because what you measure determines what you end up building.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can share general capabilities, such as reasoning with language and using tools, but does not clearly say they may share the same underlying model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that "agent" has become one word for several quite different things, and the design choices should follow the structure of the task and the mode of interaction rather than some universal template.

Let me break it down along two axes. The first is the environment: what kind of actions are available, and how fast and how clean is the feedback? Coding is the canonical example of a good environment. You have a very rich action space, but you also have compilers, tests, and runtime errors, so the agent gets grounded signal cheaply and often. In that setting you want the agent to be bold, to try things, to run them, to iterate. Long horizons are fine because every step gives you something to verify against. Web browsing or operating a GUI is the opposite in some ways. The action space is messy, the feedback is noisy, and many mistakes are hard to detect until much later. There the system needs more deliberate planning, more explicit checking of state, and probably a shorter leash in terms of how far it goes before confirming it is on track.

The second axis is the interaction mode, meaning who is in the loop and when. If a human is sitting there, like a chat interface or a pair-programming setup, the agent's job is partly to be legible. It should surface its reasoning, make small commitments, and ask when ambiguity actually matters, because the human is a cheap and high-quality source of correction. If instead the agent is running autonomously for hours, that whole strategy fails. Nobody is there to answer, so asking is just stalling. The agent has to internalize the checking role itself: decompose the task, verify intermediate results, and know when to stop and leave a clear report rather than keep going on a guess.

So concretely, I would say three things vary. One is the ratio of acting to thinking. Where feedback is cheap, act more; where it is expensive or irreversible, think more. Two is memory and context management. A short interactive session can keep everything in context, but a long autonomous run needs some notion of what to retain, what to summarize, and what to re-derive. Three is the evaluation signal you train against. For coding you can use test pass rates and get real progress. For open-ended research or ambiguous tasks, the reward is fuzzier, and you end up relying more on the model's own judgment, which means you need to invest in that judgment rather than only in tool use.

The thing I would push back on is the idea that we should build one agent framework and then just swap tools. The scaffolding that works for one regime often actively hurts in another. The interesting research question to me is less "what is the right agent architecture" and more "how does the model learn to adapt its own behavior to the environment it is in." Ideally the model itself figures out that this is a coding task with tests, so it should move quickly, versus this is a consequential action on someone's account, so it should slow down. That adaptivity, learned rather than hand-coded, is where I think the real progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response proposes that the model itself learn to adapt its behavior across task environments and interaction modes, indicating that tailored agent systems can share an underlying model.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that an agent shouldn’t have the same workflow for every task. The right system depends on how clearly the goal is specified, how easily you can check the result, and how much interaction the user wants along the way.

For coding, for example, an agent can often take an action, run a test, observe an error, and try again. That feedback loop makes relatively autonomous work possible. For an open-ended research question, even deciding what counts as a good answer may require discussion. In that setting, asking the user a useful question can be more valuable than doing another ten searches.

The interaction mode also changes the tradeoff. If I’m talking to an assistant, I want a quick response so we can keep the conversation going. If I give it a task to finish overnight, I care much more about the quality of the final result. The system should spend its time and computation differently in those two cases.

So I would separate having a general-purpose model from having one fixed agent design. The same model could support several workflows, with different tools, feedback mechanisms, and degrees of autonomy. And autonomy should be adjustable: proceed when the objective is clear and progress can be checked, and bring the user back in when a decision really depends on their preferences.

r001.rationale: The response says that the same model could support several workflows with different tools, feedback mechanisms, and degrees of autonomy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that an agent shouldn’t have the same interaction pattern for every task. Some tasks have a clear objective and a result you can verify. If you ask a coding agent to fix a bug, it can inspect the code, make a change, run tests, and iterate. In that setting, you want it to work independently for a while, because asking you about every step would defeat the purpose.

But other tasks are much more about discovering what you want. If you’re writing something together or exploring a research question, the interaction itself helps define the objective. The agent should bring back intermediate ideas, get feedback, and adjust. Running longer without talking to you doesn’t necessarily make it more useful.

So I would distinguish autonomy from how much computation the system uses. An agent might do a lot of work in the background and then give you a very concise choice. Or it might respond quickly but need several rounds of conversation. Those are different design decisions.

The key questions are: How clear is the goal? Can the agent evaluate its own progress? And how costly is a wrong action? Those should determine when it acts, when it checks its work, and when it comes back to the user.

r001.rationale: The response describes how agents should vary their interaction patterns across tasks, but it does not say or imply that those systems may share the same underlying model.
